lesson_scope: Range of trigonometric functions a + b sin(kx) and a + b cos(kx), restricted domain trigonometry, finding constants from range, forming and solving composite functions, and nested function identities.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: direct trigonometric range determination from amplitude and midline bounds.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of finding the range of a linear sine function.

hints: For all real $x$, the values of $\sin x$ oscillate strictly between $-1$ and $1$.
When $\sin x = 1$, $f(x) = 5 - 3(1) = 2$ (the minimum value).
When $\sin x = -1$, $f(x) = 5 - 3(-1) = 5 + 3 = 8$ (the maximum value).
Express the output set as a closed inequality: $2 \le f(x) \le 8$.

walkthrough.text:
Recall the standard bounds for the sine function for all real $x$:
$$-1 \le \sin x \le 1$$

Multiply through by $-3$, which reverses the inequalities:
$$-3 \le -3\sin x \le 3$$

Add $5$ to find the minimum and maximum outputs of $f(x)$:
$$5 - 3 \le 5 - 3\sin x \le 5 + 3 \implies 2 \le f(x) \le 8$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$ to obtain the extreme values $5 - 3(1) = 2$ and $5 - 3(-1) = 8$.
States the range as $2 \le f(x) \le 8$ (or $2 \le y \le 8$ or $[2, 8]$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: determining the range of a squared trigonometric function with non-negative bounds.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of squared cosine range boundaries [0, 1].

hints: Remember that squaring any real cosine value restricts the outputs to non-negative numbers: $0 \le \cos^2 x \le 1$.
Find the minimum output when $\cos^2 x = 0$: $g(x) = 4 + 7(0) = 4$.
Find the maximum output when $\cos^2 x = 1$: $g(x) = 4 + 7(1) = 11$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the range of the squared cosine term for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$:
$$0 \le \cos^2 x \le 1$$

Multiply by $7$ and add $4$ across the inequality:
$$0 \le 7\cos^2 x \le 7$$
$$4 + 0 \le 4 + 7\cos^2 x \le 4 + 7 \implies 4 \le g(x) \le 11$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies that $0 \le \cos^2 x \le 1$ for all real $x$.
Evaluates the minimum $4$ and maximum $11$ to state $4 \le g(x) \le 11$ (or $4 \le y \le 11$ or $[4, 11]$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: recovering midline and amplitude parameters from given range boundaries.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of calculating constants from trigonometric range.

hints: The maximum output occurs when $\cos x = 1$, so $p + q = 10$.
The minimum output occurs when $\cos x = -1$, so $p - q = -2$.
Add the two equations to find $2p = 8 \implies p = 4$, then subtract to find $2q = 12 \implies q = 6$.

walkthrough.text:
Use the maximum and minimum values of $\cos x = \pm 1$ to set up simultaneous equations for the range boundaries:
$$\text{Maximum: } p + q(1) = 10 \implies p + q = 10$$
$$\text{Minimum: } p + q(-1) = -2 \implies p - q = -2$$

Solve the linear system by adding and subtracting the equations:
$$(p + q) + (p - q) = 10 + (-2) \implies 2p = 8 \implies p = 4$$
$$(p + q) - (p - q) = 10 - (-2) \implies 2q = 12 \implies q = 6$$

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up equations $p + q = 10$ and $p - q = -2$ (or uses $p = \dfrac{10 + (-2)}{2}, q = \dfrac{10 - (-2)}{2}$).
Solves to obtain $p = 4$ and $q = 6$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: algebraic composition of two linear functions.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of forming linear composite functions.

prerequisite_lesson_dependency.reason: Composite function formation is controlled by M4 L1.

hints: To form $fg(x)$, replace every $x$ in $f(x)$ with the entire formula for $g(x)$.
Substitute $(5 - 2x)$ into $3x - 4$ to obtain $3(5 - 2x) - 4$.
Expand brackets: $15 - 6x - 4 = 11 - 6x$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $g(x)$ into $f(x)$:
$$fg(x) = f(g(x)) = f(5 - 2x) = 3(5 - 2x) - 4$$

Expand the bracket and collect constant terms:
$$fg(x) = 15 - 6x - 4 = 11 - 6x$$

ai_rubric.observable: Substitutes $g(x) = 5 - 2x$ into $f$: $3(5 - 2x) - 4$.
Expands and simplifies to obtain $11 - 6x$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: determining the range of a composite function by propagating an inner interval through a quadratic outer function.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of finding the range of a composite function across zero.

hints: First find the outputs of the inner function $f(x) = 2x + 1$ on $[-2, 3]$: $f(-2) = -3$ and $f(3) = 7$.
The inner outputs range across $-3 \le u \le 7$, which includes $u = 0$.
When squaring numbers in $[-3, 7]$, the minimum square is $0^2 = 0$ and the maximum square is $7^2 = 49$.
Assemble the final composite range: $0 \le gf(x) \le 49$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the output interval of the inner function $f(x) = 2x + 1$ on $-2 \le x \le 3$:
$$f(-2) = 2(-2) + 1 = -3, \qquad f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 7$$
$$\text{Range of } f: \quad -3 \le f(x) \le 7$$

Apply the outer squaring function $g(u) = u^2$ to the domain $u \in [-3, 7]$:
$$\text{Since } 0 \in [-3, 7], \text{ the minimum value is } 0^2 = 0$$
$$\text{The maximum value is } \max((-3)^2, 7^2) = 7^2 = 49$$
$$\text{Thus, the range of } gf \text{ is } 0 \le gf(x) \le 49$$

ai_rubric.observable: Finds the range of the inner function $f$ as $-3 \le f(x) \le 7$.
Applies $g(u) = u^2$ on $u \in [-3, 7]$ to obtain the range $0 \le gf(x) \le 49$ (or $0 \le y \le 49$ or $[0, 49]$).

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: identifying domain exclusions for composite functions where denominator vanishes.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Foundational check of finding input values excluded from composite domains.

prerequisite_lesson_dependency.reason: Composite domain conditions are controlled by M4 L1.

hints: The outer function $f(u) = \dfrac{1}{u - 3}$ is undefined when its input equals $3$.
Set the output of the inner function $g(x)$ equal to $3$: $2x + 7 = 3$.
Solve for $x$: $2x = 3 - 7 = -4 \implies x = -2$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the domain restriction of the outer function $f$:
$$f(u) \text{ is undefined when } u = 3$$

Set the inner function $g(x) = 2x + 7$ equal to this restricted input value $3$:
$$2x + 7 = 3$$

Solve the linear equation for $x$:
$$2x = 3 - 7 = -4 \implies x = -2$$
$$\text{Thus, } fg(x) \text{ cannot be evaluated when } x = -2$$

ai_rubric.observable: Sets the output of $g(x)$ equal to the excluded input of $f$: $2x + 7 = 3$.
Solves to obtain $x = -2$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: direct application of the trigonometric range method with a negative multiplier b = -4 and evaluation at a special angle.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the range of a trigonometric function a + b cos(kx) over a full period.

hints: For $0 \le x \le \pi$, the angle $2x$ covers $0 \le 2x \le 2\pi$, which is a complete cosine wave.
Since $-1 \le \cos 2x \le 1$, multiply through by $-4$ and remember the inequality flips direction: $-4 \le -4\cos 2x \le 4$.
Add $7$ to both boundary values to obtain the final range for $f(x)$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the range of the trigonometric component over the specified domain:
For $x \in [0, \pi]$, the angle $2x \in [0, 2\pi]$, covering a full cycle.
$$-1 \le \cos 2x \le 1$$

Multiply by $b = -4$. Because the multiplier is negative, the upper and lower bounds swap places:
$$-4(1) \le -4\cos 2x \le -4(-1)$$
$$-4 \le -4\cos 2x \le 4$$

Add the constant $a = 7$ across the entire inequality:
$$7 + (-4) \le 7 - 4\cos 2x \le 7 + 4$$
$$3 \le f(x) \le 11$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $-1 \le \cos 2x \le 1$ to the expression $7 - 4\cos 2x$, recognising that $-4 \le -4\cos 2x \le 4$.
Obtains the correct range $3 \le f(x) \le 11$ (or $3 \le y \le 11$ or $[3, 11]$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Evaluating a trigonometric function at an exact radian argument.

hints: Substitute $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into the function: $2x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Use the standard exact trigonometric value $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ into $f(x)$:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 7 - 4\cos\left(2 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 7 - 4\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

Use the exact value $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$ to compute the final result:
$$f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 7 - 4\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 7 - 2 = 5$$

ai_rubric.observable: Evaluates $f(\pi/6) = 7 - 4\cos(\pi/3) = 7 - 4(1/2) = 5$ correctly.

questions.difficulty_reason: Easy: setting up and solving a simultaneous system to determine vertical shift and amplitude from range endpoints.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding constants a and b from the stated maximum and minimum values of a trigonometric function.

hints: Since $d > 0$, the maximum of $g(x) = c + d\sin x$ occurs when $\sin x = 1$, giving $\text{max} = c + d = 9$.
The minimum occurs when $\sin x = -1$, giving $\text{min} = c - d = -3$.
Add the two equations to eliminate $d$ and find $c$, then solve for $d$.

walkthrough.text:
Relate the maximum and minimum values of the sinusoidal function to constants $c$ and $d$:
Because $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and $d > 0$,
$$\text{Maximum: } c + d = 9$$
$$\text{Minimum: } c - d = -3$$

Solve simultaneously by adding and subtracting the two equations:
$$\text{Adding: } 2c = 6 \implies c = 3$$
$$\text{Subtracting: } 2d = 12 \implies d = 6$$

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up simultaneous equations $c + d = 9$ and $c - d = -3$ from the maximum and minimum values of $g$ (or uses $c = \frac{9 + (-3)}{2}, d = \frac{9 - (-3)}{2}$).
Obtains both correct values $c = 3$ and $d = 6$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Translating the range of a sinusoidal function vertically.

hints: The new function is $h(x) = g(x) + 4$, which represents a vertical translation by $+4$.
Add $4$ to both endpoints of the range of $g(x)$ ($-3$ and $9$).

walkthrough.text:
Recognise the transformation connecting $h(x)$ and $g(x)$:
$$h(x) = (c + 4) + d\sin x = (c + d\sin x) + 4 = g(x) + 4$$

Shift the existing range $-3 \le g(x) \le 9$ upwards by $4$ units:
$$-3 + 4 \le h(x) \le 9 + 4$$
$$1 \le h(x) \le 13$$

ai_rubric.observable: States the translated range $1 \le h(x) \le 13$ by shifting the range of $g$ vertically upwards by $4$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: evaluating trigonometric range on a restricted domain with non-symmetric angle boundaries, and solving the trigonometric equation within that domain.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the range of a sine function over a restricted domain.

hints: Find the interval of the inside angle $\theta = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ when $0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Calculate $\theta$ at endpoints: $\theta(0) = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta(\pi/2) = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
Check whether the interval $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right]$ contains the maximum turning point $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Evaluate $\sin(-\pi/6) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\sin(\pi/2) = 1$ to form the output range.

walkthrough.text:
Map the domain $x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ to the inside angle $\theta = 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$\text{At } x = 0: \quad \theta = 2(0) - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}: \quad \theta = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
$$\text{Angle interval: } -\dfrac{\pi}{6} \le \theta \le \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

Find the minimum and maximum values taken by $\sin\theta$ on this interval:
- The interval passes through $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 1$ (maximum).
- The minimum occurs at the lower endpoint $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, where $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
- At the upper endpoint $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$, which is not the minimum.
$$- \dfrac{1}{2} \le \sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \le 1$$

Scale by $2$ and add $3$ to obtain the range of $f(x)$:
$$2\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \le 2\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \le 2(1)$$
$$-1 \le 2\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \le 2$$
$$3 + (-1) \le f(x) \le 3 + 2$$
$$2 \le f(x) \le 5$$

ai_rubric.observable: Determines the domain of the angle $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \le 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6} \le \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and evaluates the minimum trig value $\sin(-\pi/6) = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Identifies that the angle interval contains $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, giving the maximum trig value $\sin(\pi/2) = 1$.
Obtains the correct range $2 \le f(x) \le 5$ (or $2 \le y \le 5$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Solving a trigonometric equation within a restricted domain and expressing roots in terms of pi.

hints: Isolate the sine term: $3 + 2\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4 \implies \sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
For the angle $\theta \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right]$, identify all values where $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
The solutions for $\theta$ are $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
Set $2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \theta$ and solve for $x$ in each case.

walkthrough.text:
Isolate the trigonometric term:
$$3 + 2\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 4$$
$$2\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 1$$
$$\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Find all angle solutions in the interval $-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \le 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6} \le \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$:
$$\text{Principal angle: } \theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
$$\text{Second quadrant angle: } \theta_2 = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

Solve for $x$ from each angle value:
$$\text{Case 1: } 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{6} \implies 2x = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$$
$$\text{Case 2: } 2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \implies 2x = \dfrac{6\pi}{6} = \pi \implies x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$$
Both values lie in the domain $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

ai_rubric.observable: Rearranges $f(x) = 4$ to $\sin\left(2x - \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and finds solutions for the angle $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.
Obtains both correct values $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ within the domain $0 \le x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: algebraic composition of linear and quadratic functions in both orders, leading to a 3-term quadratic equation solved in exact surd form.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Forming and simplifying composite algebraic expressions.

hints: For $fg(x)$, substitute $g(x) = 2x^2 + 1$ into $f$: $f(g(x)) = 3(2x^2 + 1) - 2$.
For $gf(x)$, substitute $f(x) = 3x - 2$ into $g$: $g(f(x)) = 2(3x - 2)^2 + 1$.
Expand $(3x - 2)^2 = 9x^2 - 12x + 4$, multiply by $2$, and add $1$.

walkthrough.text:
Form and simplify $fg(x)$ by replacing the input of $f$ with $g(x)$:
$$fg(x) = f(2x^2 + 1) = 3(2x^2 + 1) - 2 = 6x^2 + 3 - 2 = 6x^2 + 1$$

Form and expand $gf(x)$ by replacing the input of $g$ with $f(x)$:
$$gf(x) = g(3x - 2) = 2(3x - 2)^2 + 1$$
$$gf(x) = 2(9x^2 - 12x + 4) + 1 = 18x^2 - 24x + 8 + 1 = 18x^2 - 24x + 9$$

ai_rubric.observable: Correctly determines $fg(x) = 3(2x^2 + 1) - 2 = 6x^2 + 1$.
Correctly expands and simplifies $gf(x) = 2(3x - 2)^2 + 1 = 2(9x^2 - 12x + 4) + 1 = 18x^2 - 24x + 9$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Solving an equation formed by a linear combination of composite functions.

hints: Substitute your expressions for $gf(x)$ and $fg(x)$ into the equation: $(18x^2 - 24x + 9) - 2(6x^2 + 1) = 15$.
Expand and gather all terms on one side to get a standard quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$.
Divide by the common factor to simplify to $3x^2 - 12x - 4 = 0$, then apply the quadratic formula $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute the expressions from part (a) into the given equation:
$$gf(x) - 2\,fg(x) = 15$$
$$(18x^2 - 24x + 9) - 2(6x^2 + 1) = 15$$
$$18x^2 - 24x + 9 - 12x^2 - 2 = 15$$
$$6x^2 - 24x + 7 = 15$$
$$6x^2 - 24x - 8 = 0$$

Divide by $2$ to simplify coefficients:
$$3x^2 - 12x - 4 = 0$$

Solve using the quadratic formula with $a = 3, b = -12, c = -4$:
$$x = \dfrac{-(-12) \pm \sqrt{(-12)^2 - 4(3)(-4)}}{2(3)}$$
$$x = \dfrac{12 \pm \sqrt{144 + 48}}{6} = \dfrac{12 \pm \sqrt{192}}{6}$$
$$x = \dfrac{12 \pm 8\sqrt{3}}{6} = 2 \pm \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms the equation $(18x^2 - 24x + 9) - 2(6x^2 + 1) = 15$ and simplifies to a standard 3-term quadratic $6x^2 - 24x - 8 = 0$ (or $3x^2 - 12x - 4 = 0$).
Applies the quadratic formula or completes the square to their 3-term quadratic equation.
Obtains the exact solutions $x = 2 \pm \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}$ (or equivalent simplified surd form).

questions.difficulty_reason: Medium: evaluating ranges of rational functions, composing rational functions into single fraction form, and determining the restricted domain for valid composition.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the output ranges of rational functions over asymptotic domains.

hints: For $f(x) = \dfrac{6}{x - 2}$ on $x > 2$: as $x \to 2^+$, $f(x) \to +\infty$; as $x \to +\infty$, $f(x) \to 0^+$.
For $g(x) = \dfrac{3}{2x + 1}$ on $x \ge 0$: at $x = 0$, $g(0) = 3$; as $x \to +\infty$, $g(x) \to 0^+$.
Write both ranges using strict or non-strict inequalities matching the endpoints.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the range of $f(x) = \dfrac{6}{x - 2}$ for $x > 2$:
- As $x$ approaches $2$ from the right, the denominator $x - 2 \to 0^+$, so $f(x) \to +\infty$.
- As $x \to +\infty$, $x - 2 \to +\infty$, so $f(x) \to 0^+$.
- Because $x > 2$ is strictly greater, $f(x)$ takes all strictly positive real values:
$$\text{Range of } f: \quad f(x) > 0$$

Determine the range of $g(x) = \dfrac{3}{2x + 1}$ for $x \ge 0$:
- At the boundary $x = 0$, $g(0) = \dfrac{3}{2(0) + 1} = 3$ (maximum value).
- As $x \to +\infty$, $2x + 1 \to +\infty$, so $g(x) \to 0^+$.
- Thus, the output takes values between $0$ (exclusive) and $3$ (inclusive):
$$\text{Range of } g: \quad 0 < g(x) \le 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: States the correct range of $f$ as $f(x) > 0$ (or $y > 0$).
States the correct range of $g$ as $0 < g(x) \le 3$ (or $0 < y \le 3$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Composing rational functions and simplifying compound fractions.

hints: Substitute $f(x)$ into $g(x)$: $gf(x) = \dfrac{3}{2\left(\dfrac{6}{x-2}\right) + 1}$.
Simplify the denominator by writing $1 = \dfrac{x-2}{x-2}$: $\dfrac{12}{x-2} + 1 = \dfrac{12 + x - 2}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 10}{x - 2}$.
Multiply numerator and denominator by $(x - 2)$ to clear the inner fraction.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute $f(x)$ into the expression for $g(x)$:
$$gf(x) = g\left(\dfrac{6}{x-2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2\left(\dfrac{6}{x-2}\right) + 1} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{12}{x-2} + 1}$$

Combine terms in the denominator over the common denominator $(x - 2)$:
$$\dfrac{12}{x-2} + 1 = \dfrac{12 + (x - 2)}{x - 2} = \dfrac{x + 10}{x - 2}$$

Invert and multiply to clear the fraction:
$$gf(x) = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{x + 10}{x - 2}} = \dfrac{3(x - 2)}{x + 10} = \dfrac{3x - 6}{x + 10}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Substitutes $f(x) = \dfrac{6}{x-2}$ into $g(x)$ to form $\dfrac{3}{2\left(\frac{6}{x-2}\right) + 1}$ and puts denominator over common denominator $(x-2)$.
Simplifies to obtain $gf(x) = \dfrac{3x - 6}{x + 10}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Determining domain restrictions ensuring the output of the inner function meets the domain of the outer function.

hints: For $fg(x) = f(g(x))$ to be defined, the output $g(x)$ must lie inside the domain of $f$, which requires $g(x) > 2$.
Since the range of $g$ is $0 < g(x) \le 3$, some outputs are $\le 2$, meaning $f(g(x))$ is undefined for those $x$.
Set $\dfrac{3}{2x + 1} > 2$, multiply by the positive denominator $2x + 1$, and solve for $x$ given $x \ge 0$.

walkthrough.text:
State the condition required for composition:
For $fg(x)$ to exist, every output of the inner function $g$ must fall within the domain of the outer function $f$.
$$\text{Domain of } f: \quad u > 2 \implies g(x) > 2$$
Because the range of $g$ on $x \ge 0$ is $0 < g(x) \le 3$, values of $g(x) \le 2$ cannot be evaluated by $f$.

Solve the inequality $g(x) > 2$ for $x \ge 0$:
$$\dfrac{3}{2x + 1} > 2$$
Since $x \ge 0$, $2x + 1 > 0$, so we multiply without reversing the inequality:
$$3 > 2(2x + 1)$$
$$3 > 4x + 2$$
$$4x < 1 \implies x < \dfrac{1}{4}$$

Combine with the natural domain $x \ge 0$:
$$0 \le x < \dfrac{1}{4}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that for $fg(x)$ to exist, the range of $g$ must fall within the domain of $f$ ($g(x) > 2$), and sets $\dfrac{3}{2x+1} > 2$.
Solves $\dfrac{3}{2x+1} > 2$ to obtain the complete valid domain $0 \le x < \dfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: equating coefficients of nested radical expressions to find constants, tracking domain/range through composite transformation, and determining domain threshold for one-one behavior.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding parameters by comparing a composite expression g(h(x)) to a target function f(x).

hints: Substitute $h(x) = \sqrt{x} - 2$ into $g(u) = pu^2 + q$: $g(h(x)) = p(\sqrt{x} - 2)^2 + q$.
Expand $(\sqrt{x} - 2)^2 = (\sqrt{x})^2 - 4\sqrt{x} + 4 = x - 4\sqrt{x} + 4$.
Multiply by $p$ and add $q$: $g(h(x)) = px - 4p\sqrt{x} + (4p + q)$.
Equate coefficients with $f(x) = 2x - 8\sqrt{x} + 11$ to solve for $p$ and $q$.

walkthrough.text:
Express $g(h(x))$ algebraically:
$$g(h(x)) = g(\sqrt{x} - 2) = p(\sqrt{x} - 2)^2 + q$$

Expand the squared bracket:
$$(\sqrt{x} - 2)^2 = x - 4\sqrt{x} + 4$$
$$g(h(x)) = p(x - 4\sqrt{x} + 4) + q = px - 4p\sqrt{x} + 4p + q$$

Match coefficients with $f(x) = 2x - 8\sqrt{x} + 11$:
$$\text{Coefficient of } x: \quad p = 2$$
$$\text{Coefficient of } \sqrt{x}: \quad -4p = -8 \implies p = 2 \quad \text{(consistent)}$$
$$\text{Constant term: } \quad 4p + q = 11 \implies 4(2) + q = 11 \implies 8 + q = 11 \implies q = 3$$
$$p = 2, \quad q = 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: Forms $g(h(x)) = p(\sqrt{x} - 2)^2 + q$ and expands to $p(x - 4\sqrt{x} + 4) + q = px - 4p\sqrt{x} + 4p + q$.
Equates coefficients of $x$ (or $\sqrt{x}$) and constant terms with $2x - 8\sqrt{x} + 11$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the range of a composite function by finding the range of the inner function first.

hints: For $h(x) = \sqrt{x} - 2$ with $x \ge 0$, the smallest value occurs when $x = 0$, giving $h(0) = -2$.
As $x \to \infty$, $\sqrt{x} \to \infty$, so the range of $h$ is $h(x) \ge -2$.
Now consider $g(u) = 2u^2 + 3$ on the domain $u \ge -2$.
The minimum of the parabola $2u^2 + 3$ occurs at $u = 0$, which is inside $[-2, \infty)$, giving minimum output $g(0) = 3$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the range of the inner function $h(x) = \sqrt{x} - 2$ for $x \ge 0$:
Since $\sqrt{x} \ge 0$ for all $x \ge 0$,
$$\sqrt{x} - 2 \ge -2$$
$$\text{Range of } h: \quad h(x) \ge -2 \quad (\text{or } u \in [-2, \infty))$$

Evaluate the outer function $g(u) = 2u^2 + 3$ over the domain $u \ge -2$:
- The parabola $g(u) = 2u^2 + 3$ has its global vertex at $u = 0$.
- Since $u = 0$ lies in the interval $[-2, \infty)$, the minimum value of $g(u)$ is attained at $u = 0$:
$$g(0) = 2(0)^2 + 3 = 3$$
- As $u \to \infty$, $g(u) \to \infty$.
$$\text{Range of } f: \quad f(x) \ge 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: States the range of $h$ as $h(x) \ge -2$ (or $[-2, \infty)$).
Uses the minimum value of $g(u) = 2u^2 + 3$ at $u = 0$ (which lies in $u \ge -2$) to state the range of $f$ as $f(x) \ge 3$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Explaining why a function is not one-to-one and finding the domain restriction for an inverse to exist.

hints: A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one.
On $x \ge 0$, $u = \sqrt{x} - 2$ takes values in $[-2, \infty)$, which contains values on both sides of the turning point $u = 0$.
For example, $u = -1$ (at $x = 1$) and $u = 1$ (at $x = 9$) both produce $f = 5$, showing $f$ is many-to-one.
To make $f$ one-to-one, we must restrict to $u \ge 0$, which gives $\sqrt{x} - 2 \ge 0 \implies x \ge 4$, so $k = 4$.

walkthrough.text:
Explain why $f$ is not one-to-one on the domain $x \ge 0$:
A function has an inverse if and only if it is one-to-one. On the domain $x \ge 0$, the intermediate variable $u = \sqrt{x} - 2$ spans $[-2, \infty)$, which includes the turning point $u = 0$ of the quadratic $g(u) = 2u^2 + 3$.
Because the domain contains values on both sides of the vertex $u = 0$, $f$ is many-to-one (e.g. $f(1) = f(9) = 5$), so no inverse exists.

Determine the minimum domain threshold $k$ for one-to-one behavior:
To ensure $f$ is one-to-one, we must restrict $u$ to the monotonic increasing branch $u \ge 0$:
$$u \ge 0 \implies \sqrt{x} - 2 \ge 0$$
$$\sqrt{x} \ge 2 \implies x \ge 4$$
Thus, the least value of $k$ is $k = 4$.

ai_rubric.observable: Explains that $f$ is many-to-one on $x \ge 0$ because the vertex $u = 0$ corresponds to an interior point $x = 4$.
States the least value of $k$ is $4$ (corresponding to restricting $u \ge 0$ so that the function is strictly increasing).

questions.difficulty_reason: Hard: analyzing range of squared trigonometric function, finding exact radians from quadratic trig equation, and feeding trig range into a radical composite function.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the range of a squared trigonometric function a - b sin^2(x).

hints: For $0 \le x \le \pi$, the sine function takes values $0 \le \sin x \le 1$.
Squaring this interval gives $0^2 \le \sin^2 x \le 1^2$, so $0 \le \sin^2 x \le 1$.
Multiply by $-8$ (flip inequality): $-8 \le -8\sin^2 x \le 0$.
Add $5$ to obtain the complete output range for $f(x)$.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the range of the squared trigonometric term on $[0, \pi]$:
For $x \in [0, \pi]$, the sine function ranges from $0$ (at $x = 0, \pi$) to $1$ (at $x = \pi/2$):
$$0 \le \sin x \le 1$$
Squaring gives:
$$0 \le \sin^2 x \le 1$$

Apply the linear scaling and translation:
Multiply by $-8$ (reversing the bounds):
$$-8(1) \le -8\sin^2 x \le -8(0) \implies -8 \le -8\sin^2 x \le 0$$
Add $5$:
$$5 + (-8) \le 5 - 8\sin^2 x \le 5 + 0$$
$$-3 \le f(x) \le 5$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies that for $0 \le x \le \pi$, $0 \le \sin^2 x \le 1$, so $-8 \le -8\sin^2 x \le 0$.
Obtains the correct range $-3 \le f(x) \le 5$ (or $[-3, 5]$).

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Solving a squared trigonometric equation for exact radian values.

hints: Set $5 - 8\sin^2 x = -1$ and isolate $\sin^2 x$: $8\sin^2 x = 6 \implies \sin^2 x = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
Take the square root: $\sin x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (reject negative root since $\sin x \ge 0$ on $[0, \pi]$).
Find all angles in $[0, \pi]$ satisfying $\sin x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ in exact multiples of $\pi$.

walkthrough.text:
Rearrange the equation to isolate $\sin^2 x$:
$$5 - 8\sin^2 x = -1$$
$$8\sin^2 x = 6$$
$$\sin^2 x = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$$

Take the square root, noting that $\sin x \ge 0$ on the domain $0 \le x \le \pi$:
$$\sin x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

Solve for all solutions in $0 \le x \le \pi$:
$$\text{Principal solution: } x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
$$\text{Second quadrant solution: } x = \pi - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Rearranges $5 - 8\sin^2 x = -1$ to obtain $\sin^2 x = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\sin x = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (rejecting negative root for $0 \le x \le \pi$).
Obtains the first solution $x = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
Obtains the second solution $x = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Finding the output range of a composite function h(f(x)) where the inner function is trigonometric.

hints: The composite function is $hf(x) = h(f(x)) = \sqrt{f(x) + 4}$.
From part (a), the range of $f(x)$ is $-3 \le f(x) \le 5$.
Substitute this range into the argument of $h$: $-3 + 4 \le f(x) + 4 \le 5 + 4 \implies 1 \le f(x) + 4 \le 9$.
Take the square root of both bounds: $\sqrt{1} \le hf(x) \le \sqrt{9}$.

walkthrough.text:
Write the composite function expression:
$$hf(x) = h(f(x)) = \sqrt{f(x) + 4}$$
From part (a), the set of outputs from $f(x)$ on $0 \le x \le \pi$ is $-3 \le f(x) \le 5$.

Evaluate the range of the expression inside the square root:
$$-3 + 4 \le f(x) + 4 \le 5 + 4$$
$$1 \le f(x) + 4 \le 9$$

Apply the square root function across the inequality:
Because $y = \sqrt{u}$ is strictly increasing for $u \ge 0$:
$$\sqrt{1} \le \sqrt{f(x) + 4} \le \sqrt{9}$$
$$1 \le hf(x) \le 3$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies the range of $f$ ($-3 \le f(x) \le 5$) into $h(u) = \sqrt{u + 4}$, identifying input interval $[1, 9]$ for the square root.
Evaluates $\sqrt{1} = 1$ and $\sqrt{9} = 3$ to obtain the range $1 \le hf(x) \le 3$ (or $[1, 3]$).
